catalog_quote: The most common stress pattern in Toto-Zoquean is primary stress on the final heavy syllable, but otherwise on the penult, as in Sierra Popoluca (de Jong Boudreault 2009), Misantla Totonac (MacKay 1999), Pisaflores Tepehua (MacKay & Treschel 2013), Huehuetla Totonac (Kung 2007), and Texistepec Popoluca (Wichmann 1994). The phonological criteria for categorizing syllables as light or heavy varies by language. In Pisaflores Tepehua, syllables with long vowels and/or sonorant codas are heavy, but syllables with obstruent codas are light (MacKay & Treschel 2013). ... Primary stress is assigned at the right edge, but secondary stress surfaces on all preceding heavy syllables in the word, a pattern also observed in Pisaflores Totonac (MacKay & Treschel 2013).

The phonological criteria for categorizing syllables as light or heavy varies by langu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable if it is heavy (long vowel and/or sonorant coda); otherwise on the penult. Syllables closed by an obstruent count as light. Secondary stress on every preceding heavy syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Lines 550-552: 'Primary stress is assigned at the right edge, but secondary stress surfaces on all preceding heavy syllables in the word, a pattern also observed in Pisaflores Totonac (MacKay & Treschel 2013).' ('Pisaflores Totonac' here is a slip for Pisaflores Tepehua.)
new_statements.exceptions: None specific to Pisaflores Tepehua; the chapter notes generally that 'morpheme-specific exceptions to these stress patterns occur throughout the family' (lines 559-560).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress ('primary stress usually surfaces at the right edge of the morphological word', line 538); the chapter summarizes the whole Toto-Zoquean group and gives no Pisaflores Tepehua examples, so the exact domain (stem vs. word with affixes/clitics) and any morphological conditions must be checked in MacKay & Trechsel 2013.
new_statements.identity_note: Pisaflores Tepehua (pisa1237, ISO tpp), spoken in Pisaflores, Ixhuatlan de Madero, Veracruz; MacKay & Trechsel's data are from this variety. DiCanio & Bennett once write 'Pisaflores Totonac' and spell the author 'Treschel' -- both slips for Pisaflores Tepehua / Trechsel. Not to be confused with Huehuetla Tepehua (hueh1236, incl. Mecapalapa) or Tlachichilco Tepehua (tlac1235).

new_statements.quote: [fn. 4, p. 125] Only the right-most stressed syllable receives primary stress in Totonac and Tepehua. All other stressed syllables receive secondary stress. [fn. 5, p. 126] Evidence of the unitary status of /kin=laa-/ is the lack of secondary stress on the first syllable, [kiláa-]. If the prefix were underlyingly /kin-laa-/ with a closed first syllable, both syllables would be stressed. [p. 137] In the following examples, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, which is expected if the final syllable ends in an obstruent. [fn. 16, p. 148] Throughout the family, when there is a word-final CV syllable, stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable. In the examples in (73), the underlying word-final [y] attracts stress to the word-final syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: First-hand statements by the describers of Pisaflores Tepehua (the authors of the closed MacKay & Trechsel 2013 IJAL sketch). Compatible with the existing weight-sensitive statement (DiCanio & Bennett 2020, second-hand: final heavy else penult, secondary stress on preceding heavy syllables): it corroborates the closed-syllable = heavy criterion for a Pisaflores form, the secondary-stress pattern, the obstruent-coda-is-light observation, and the final-CV -> penult default. It is partial (footnotes, mostly family-wide) and fills the catalog record's empty rule field rather than contradicting anything. Does not settle whether a final long vowel alone attracts primary stress in Pisaflores (the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No dedicated stress section: the paper is a comparative-classification study and states stress only in footnotes and asides, family-wide, with Pisaflores Tepehua as its Tepehua exemplar. What it says: closed (CVC) syllables are stressed (fn. 5, on a Pisaflores form); of the stressed syllables the rightmost carries primary stress and all others secondary (fn. 4); a word-final open CV syllable does not take stress, so stress falls on the penult (fn. 16); a final syllable closed by an obstruent also yields penult primary stress (p. 137, Totonac examples), while an underlying final sonorant /y/ attracts stress to the final syllable (fn. 16). Together: primary stress on the final syllable when it is heavy (sonorant-closed; long vowels are stressed in the cited forms), otherwise on the penult, with secondary stress on other heavy syllables. The paper never assembles this into a single Pisaflores-specific rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly (fn. 4, p. 125): every stressed (heavy) syllable other than the rightmost receives secondary stress; fn. 5 (p. 126) uses the absence of secondary stress on [kiláa-] to argue the prefix's first syllable is not closed.
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 16 (p. 148): in Northern, Papantla and Misantla Totonac an underlying word-final /y/ (deleted on the surface) attracts stress to a surface-final open syllable (chipá, taštú, ¢ukú); this is a Totonac, not Pisaflores, exception. Pisaflores keeps final [y] on the surface with final stress ([č’uk’úy], ex. 19, p. 131), consistent with a sonorant coda counting heavy.
new_statements.identity_note: The work is a comparative study of the whole Totonac-Tepehua family. Its stress statements at fn. 4 (p. 125), p. 137 and fn. 16 (p. 148) are phrased for 'Totonac and Tepehua' / 'throughout the family'; only fn. 5 (p. 126) and the stressed example forms (exx. 1-19, pp. 125-131; wordlist ex. 84, p. 153) are specifically Pisaflores Tepehua (Pisaflores, Veracruz = pisa1237 [tpp]). The p. 137 examples are Ozelonacaxtla and Filomeno Mata Totonac, and the fn. 16 final-/y/ exception concerns Northern/Papantla/Misantla Totonac, not Pisaflores.
